problem: RL target-driven navigation (e.g. Zhu et al. 2017 siamese A3C) drops sharply on goals unseen in training, and earlier successor-representation work was DQN-based and only shown in simple maze-like worlds. Universal Successor Representations (USR) combined naively with A3C were unstable in a photo-realistic environment.
motivation: Value functions and rewards are defined per goal, so agents struggle to transfer across goals. Successor representations decouple environment dynamics from the reward, so learned dynamics could transfer to new targets. Making this work with scalable actor-critic training in photo-realistic scenes is a step toward real-world assistive agents.
key_idea: Combine USR with A3C by pretraining a robust state representation with auxiliary dynamics losses and training the policy with a hybrid advantage that mixes the ordinary scalar-reward advantage and the successor-feature advantage.
insight: Keeping the conventional value loss alongside the SR loss stabilizes training. The SR loss never reaches zero but is enough to give generalization, and value loss rises after lambda is increased, showing the SR term affects learning. The paper reports no ablations or baseline comparisons (it explicitly skips an A3C baseline), so the evidence is qualitative.
method: State representation network: an autoencoder trained with added forward-dynamics (MSE) and inverse-dynamics (cross-entropy) auxiliary losses to give a robust feature phi, pretrained on random-policy rollouts
Reward prediction network: a 3-layer CNN maps the goal image to a reward weight vector omega_g so that r_g ≈ phi(s')^T omega_g; pretrained on rollouts, then trained jointly with the agent
RL network: a shared 3-layer siamese CNN encodes the current state and goal image, followed by FC layers; heads output policy pi, value V, and a USR approximator psi
Hybrid advantage: a weighted sum, with weight lambda, of the SF advantage [phi(s_t)+gamma psi(s_{t+1})-psi(s_t)]^T omega_g and the standard discounted-return advantage
Training schedule: lambda starts very low, then rises to 0.001 after 5k iterations with 32 asynchronous agents; total loss = lambda*L_psi + L_V + L_pi + L_H
Transfer: fine-tune the trained network on new goals (under 15 minutes)

setting.backbone: 3-layer siamese CNN + FC actor-critic (A3C) with USR head, trained from scratch
setting.training_data: RL in one AI2-THOR scene (Bathroom 02, 180 states) with 5 training goals; random-policy rollouts for pretraining the state and reward networks
setting.observation: 4 stacked 110x110 grayscale frames (downscaled from 300x400 RGB), goal given as an image
setting.action_space: 4 discrete actions: forward 0.5 m, backward 0.5 m, turn left, turn right, on a 0.5 m grid

numbers_note: Results are only shown in figures (per-goal success rate over 50 goals, 100 episodes each, 500-step limit; fine-tuning curve); no numeric tables or text values.
results: After training on 5 goals in one scene, the agent reached 19+ unseen goals without extra training, with success rates given per goal in a figure. Fine-tuning on new goals it had failed on succeeded in under 15 minutes. No baselines were compared (e.g. Zhu et al. 2017 or plain A3C).
limitations: Single scene, 5 training goals, and no baseline or ablation comparisons; results are qualitative and appear only in figures
Success rate on many unseen goals is imperfect; the SR loss does not converge to zero and training needs staged pretraining and a lambda schedule
Simulation only on a discrete grid; no real-robot evaluation
compares_to: Zhang et al. 2017 (DQN-based SR, discussed only)
